strengths: Clearly identifies a real and practically important bottleneck in Neural CDEs: solver NFE is coupled to the roughness of the interpolated control path, and provides a coherent theoretical narrative (Sec 3.2-3.4, Appendix A) linking path derivative bounds to solver step size and NFE.

The proposed combination of GP/kernel smoothing with a Q-Former-style multi-query attention mechanism to recover information lost to smoothing is a reasonable and moderately novel architectural idea, including a convolutional variant (MVC-CDE) and heteroscedastic-noise weighted GP paths that adapt precision per attention head.

Fairly comprehensive empirical study: main accuracy/efficiency comparison (Table 1), Pareto plots against multiple baselines, noise-robustness sweeps, head-count ablations, bandwidth-initialization ablations (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous), attention visualizations, and a granular training-time/overhead breakdown.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information: dataset splits, normalization, padding strategy, architecture sizes, optimizer settings, and per-dataset hyperparameters are reported in the appendix.
Reported speedups (4.3x-14.5x) alongside accuracy improvements over spline-based Neural CDE baselines are a meaningful practical contribution if they hold up.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is limited to three UEA classification datasets of modest size; no forecasting tasks, no larger-scale or higher-stakes datasets (e.g., the medical/financial applications motivated in the introduction) are used, which limits the evidence for generality and significance of the claimed 'SOTA' results.

Several 'theorems' (3.1, 3.2) are informal restatements of standard numerical-analysis and GP-regression facts (LTE scaling with derivative order, RBF derivative bounds, BLUP optimality of GP mean) rather than novel technical results; presenting them as formal theorems risks overstating the paper's theoretical originality.

Theorem 3.4 shows NFE is bottlenecked by the smallest bandwidth among heads, yet the best reported configurations (e.g., MVC-CDE main model uses uniformly large bandwidths like 166.6 across all heads) largely avoid this regime, raising the question of whether the multi-head mechanism is genuinely recovering fine-grained information or mostly aggregating similarly coarse views; this tension between the theory and the chosen operating point is not discussed.

Hyperparameter tuning appears asymmetric across baselines: ODE-RNN, GRU-D, and Log-NCDE receive dataset-specific learning-rate/tolerance search, while Linear/Cubic and the proposed methods share a fixed schedule, which complicates a strictly fair comparison and makes it hard to attribute gains purely to the proposed path construction.

The discrete-time GRU-D baseline achieves highly competitive accuracy at a fraction of the time/NFE cost of any continuous-time model (including the proposed one) on some datasets, which is not discussed and somewhat undercuts the paper's framing of continuous-time smoothing as the key lever for efficient sequence modeling.

The rectilinear zero-derivative padding scheme for variable-length sequences could artificially reduce NFE for all methods in a way that is not clearly disentangled from the proposed smoothing benefits, particularly for SpokenArabicDigits where sequence lengths vary widely (4-93).

No mention of code release; despite detailed hyperparameter tables, full reproducibility (e.g., exact implementation of the weighted GP/kernel paths and multi-head integration) is not guaranteed without released code.
The Impact Statement is generic boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any limitations or potential negative consequences of the work.

Comparisons to other efficiency-oriented Neural CDE variants (e.g., Neural Rough CDEs, seminorm-based tolerance relaxation) are discussed qualitatively in related work but not included as empirical baselines, leaving open how the proposed method compares quantitatively to these alternative efficiency strategies.

strengths: The core idea—replacing exact spline interpolation with smoothing priors (kernel/GP) to decouple NFE from input noise, combined with a learnable multi-head attention mechanism to recover information lost to smoothing—is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated combination of ideas from nonparametric regression and Q-Former-style attention.

The paper provides an explicit (if informal) theoretical link between control-path derivative norms and solver NFE (Theorem 3.1) and derives bandwidth-dependent bounds for kernel/GP smoothed paths (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3), giving some analytical grounding for the claimed speedups.

The empirical package is fairly extensive: Pareto efficiency plots, noise-robustness sweeps, head-count/bandwidth ablations, attention visualizations, and a detailed cost breakdown (trajectory-fit vs. training vs. inference) are all included, and Appendix B documents hyperparameters and settings in useful detail for reproducibility.
Reported speedups (4.3x-14.5x) and accuracy gains over Linear/Cubic Neural CDE and Log-NCDE baselines on the three chosen datasets are reasonably large and consistent across datasets.
weaknesses: Motivation-evaluation mismatch: the introduction and related work repeatedly emphasize Neural CDEs' advantage for irregularly-sampled and missing real-world data (medical records, sensor failures), yet Appendix B.2 states the datasets are padded to regular grids with fixed ∆t=1 and no missing values are simulated or evaluated. The central practical justification for Neural CDEs is therefore untested, undermining the significance of the claimed contribution.

Missing directly relevant baselines: the related-work section explicitly discusses ContiFormer, Attentive NCDEs (Jhin et al. 2024), EXIT-NCDE, Neural Lad, DeNOTS, Neural Rough CDEs, and Structured Linear CDEs as closely related attention-based or algebraic-efficiency approaches to Neural CDEs, but none of these are included as empirical baselines. Given that the paper's stated novelty is specifically attention-as-reconstruction versus attention-as-temporal-modeling in these prior works, the absence of any direct empirical comparison is a significant evidentiary gap.

Potential unfairness in the comparison of ablation configurations: the primary MVC-GP model (Table 1) is reported with substantially different, apparently separately hand-tuned bandwidth configurations for each dataset (e.g., all four heads at BW=166.6 for CharacterTrajectories) than the single-path Gaussian/GP or MV variants, making it unclear whether gains stem from the multi-view attention mechanism itself or simply from a more extensive/favorable hyperparameter search for the headline configuration.

The theoretical proofs in Appendix A are informal and rely on unproven proportionality assumptions (e.g., "assuming fθ is Lipschitz continuous and bounded, we have ||d^(p+1)z/dt^(p+1)|| ∝ ||d^(p+1)X/dt^(p+1)||" is stated without derivation, and the interaction between the vector field's own derivatives and the control path's derivatives via the chain rule is not rigorously handled). Theorem 3.4's bottleneck prediction (NFE governed by min_m h_m) is also not clearly validated against Table 1, where the main MVC-GP configuration achieves lower NFE than single-path models despite using multiple heads.

Only three UEA benchmarks are used, all relatively small and short (max length 315), none of which contain missing observations or irregular sampling; results may not generalize to larger, noisier, or more irregular real-world time series that motivate the paper (e.g., clinical/EHR data explicitly cited in the introduction).

No explicit Limitations section; the boilerplate Impact Statement ("none which we feel must be specifically highlighted") does not engage with actual limitations such as the added hyperparameter burden (M, h per head, kernel choice), GP's O(N^3) preprocessing scalability to longer sequences, or the untested irregular/missing-data setting.

Marginal statistical separation in several comparisons (e.g., MV-GP 92.97±1.74 vs. MVC-Gaussian 91.71±1.40 vs. GP CDE 88.15±0.42 on CharacterTrajectories) raises questions about the robustness of ranking claims given only 5 seeds and no significance testing.

The surprisingly strong and highly efficient performance of the simple discrete-time GRU-D baseline (near-top accuracy on 2 of 3 datasets, negligible training time, since it bypasses ODE solving entirely) is not critically discussed, which somewhat undercuts the narrative that continuous-time CDE machinery (even the proposed efficient variant) is clearly the preferred practical choice on these benchmarks.

strengths: Clearly motivated problem: the paper correctly identifies that NFE in Neural CDEs is driven by the roughness/high-order derivatives of the interpolated control path, and builds a coherent story from this observation to a concrete architectural fix (kernel/GP smoothing + attentive multi-view recovery).

The theoretical section (Theorem 3.1–3.4, Appendix A) provides an explicit, internally consistent chain of reasoning linking solver step-size control, kernel/GP derivative bounds, and the resulting NFE scaling with bandwidth h, including an interesting 'bottleneck' result for the multi-head block-diagonal system (NFE governed by the smallest hm).

The empirical evaluation is reasonably comprehensive for the claimed scope: three datasets with distinct characteristics (dimensionality, sequence length, noise), a Pareto-efficiency comparison against multiple established baselines (Linear/Cubic NCDE, ODE-RNN, GRU-D, Log-NCDE), an explicit noise-robustness stress test, head-count/bandwidth ablations, attention visualizations, and a granular wall-clock time breakdown separating pre-computation from iterative training cost.

Reported gains are substantial and consistent across datasets (higher accuracy and 4.3x–14.5x speedups over standard NCDEs), and the noise-robustness experiment directly supports the central claim that smoothing decouples NFE from input noise, unlike exact interpolation.

Good positioning relative to related work (signature-based methods, Neural SDEs, continuous attention models), with a clear articulation of what is novel (using attention for path reconstruction/recovery rather than temporal dependency modeling).
Appendix provides detailed hyperparameters and dataset-specific settings, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to three small-to-moderate UEA classification benchmarks; despite motivating the work with medical, financial, and physical time-series applications (which are typically forecasting/regression and irregularly sampled with missing data), no forecasting or irregularly-sampled/missing-data experiment is included, limiting evidence for the claimed general applicability of the method.

The theoretical results, while appealingly rigorous in appearance, rely on informal approximations (e.g., 'Theorem' 3.1 assumes state derivatives scale proportionally to control derivatives via an unproven Lipschitz/boundedness argument, and the LTE-to-NFE integral conversion glosses over the discrete nature of adaptive stepping); the paper does not empirically verify the predicted NFE ∝ h^{-1} scaling law directly, leaving the theory somewhat decoupled from the experiments.

The heteroscedastic noise construction for the Weighted GP Path (inverse relationship between attention score and noise variance) is a heuristic without a formal justification connecting it to a well-posed probabilistic model; it is unclear whether this yields the theoretically 'optimal' smoothing claimed elsewhere in the paper (Appendix A.5's optimality argument concerns single-path GP vs. kernel smoothing, not the weighted multi-head variant actually used).

Missing comparisons against several efficiency-oriented baselines explicitly discussed in Related Work (Neural Rough CDEs, Structured Linear CDEs, Neural Flows) and continuous-attention baselines (ContiFormer, Attentive NCDEs), despite these being the most relevant competitors to the paper's efficiency and attention-based claims.

GRU-D, a much simpler discrete recurrent baseline, achieves highly competitive accuracy (e.g., 96.57% vs. MVC-GP's 98.28% on SpokenArabicDigits) at a small fraction of the training time (2.02s vs. 7.32s), which somewhat undercuts the 'efficiency' framing of the paper's headline speedup claims against continuous-time baselines only; this comparison and its implications are not discussed.

GP-based smoothing has O(N^3) preprocessing cost; while claimed 'negligible,' this is only empirically demonstrated on sequences up to 315 steps, and no scaling analysis is given for longer sequences where this could become a genuine bottleneck.

The paper offers limited discussion of failure modes or scenarios where over-smoothing/attention recovery could fail (e.g., tasks requiring exact reproduction of extreme/rare spikes), and the Impact Statement is boilerplate with no substantive discussion of limitations or ethical considerations.

No mention of code release, and while hyperparameters are extensively documented, the complexity of the multi-view weighted GP/kernel construction combined with numerous dataset-specific hyperparameters (varying per dataset) raises some reproducibility concerns absent public code.

strengths: Clearly identifies and motivates a real, practically important bottleneck for Neural CDEs: exact interpolation of noisy data induces high-frequency path variation that forces adaptive solvers into small steps, inflating NFE.

Provides a coherent theoretical narrative connecting solver local truncation error, control-path derivative bounds, and smoothing bandwidth (Theorems 3.1-3.4), giving at least heuristic justification for why smoothing should reduce NFE and why multi-head integration is bottlenecked by the smallest bandwidth.

Extensive empirical evaluation: three UEA classification benchmarks, an ETTm1 forecasting task under missingness, noise-robustness sweeps, head-count/bandwidth ablations, solver-order sensitivity, high-dimensional scalability (PEMS-SF, 963 dims), memory/parameter comparisons against Mamba, attention-diversity regularization studies, and comparison against a traditional smoothing-spline baseline — this breadth supports the central claims reasonably well.

Reports consistent and fairly large speedups (NFE and wall-clock) alongside accuracy improvements over spline-based Neural CDE baselines, with capacity-matched baselines to isolate the effect of path construction.
Reasonably detailed appendix with hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and preprocessing, aiding reproducibility.
Honest limitations section acknowledging solver dependency, bandwidth tuning burden, stiffest-head bottleneck, and residual information loss.
weaknesses: The core theoretical derivations rely on informal steps (e.g., assuming derivatives of the latent state scale linearly with derivatives of the driving path via an unstated Lipschitz/boundedness argument, despite the CDE dynamics being explicitly stated as multiplicative/nonlinear) — the rigor suggested by the 'Theorem' labeling exceeds what is actually proven, and tightness/constants are never validated empirically against the derived scaling laws.

The claimed optimality of GP smoothing (Appendix A.5) is proven only relative to Nadaraya-Watson under a linear-smoother framework with a fixed bandwidth and known noise variance; this is a narrow comparison that doesn't clearly establish superiority over other smoothing/regularization schemes in practice, and the empirical gap between GP and Kernel variants is sometimes small.

GP posterior computation has cubic cost in sequence length, dismissed as 'negligible one-time preprocessing,' but this is not rigorously benchmarked for longer sequences than those used (max length ~315), leaving scalability to longer real-world sequences (e.g., long clinical time series) unaddressed.

Benchmarks are relatively small and standard UEA classification sets; PEMS-SF has only 440 samples, and Speech Commands/forecasting experiments are compared against a narrow baseline set (GRU, Cubic NCDE) rather than strong modern forecasting baselines, limiting the generality of the 'SOTA' and 'competitive with Mamba' claims (Mamba in fact outperforms the proposed method on CharacterTrajectories).

Hyperparameter tuning appears asymmetric across methods: the proposed models and Linear/Cubic CDE baselines share a fixed training schedule while other baselines (ODE-RNN, GRU-D, Log-NCDE, Mamba) were tuned separately per dataset; while justified as isolating path-construction effects, this could still bias comparisons, and the degree of tuning effort for the proposed method's own many hyperparameters (bandwidth, noise, kernel size, per-head schedules) versus baselines is not clearly equalized.

The architectural novelty is somewhat incremental — it largely combines existing ingredients (kernel/GP smoothing, Q-Former-style cross-attention, block-diagonal parallel ODE integration from prior work) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper's own related-work section acknowledges most components are adaptations of prior techniques.

The attention-diversity ablation (Table 4) shows that explicitly encouraging head diversity actually harms accuracy, which somewhat undercuts the narrative that attention heads are learning complementary, interpretable multi-scale representations rather than being an incidental ensembling effect.
No explicit statement of code/data release, which combined with the many finely-tuned hyperparameters (per-dataset, per-head bandwidths) raises reproducibility concerns despite the detailed appendix.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and well-motivated practical bottleneck of Neural CDEs: NFE explosion caused by the roughness of exact interpolants used to build the driving control path.

The theoretical framing connecting local truncation error, solver order, and the (p+1)-th derivative of the control path (Theorem 3.1) is a reasonable, if somewhat standard, way to explain why smoothing should reduce NFE, and the derivative bounds for kernel/GP smoothers (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3) are intuitive and clearly derived.

The experimental protocol is unusually extensive for a single paper: noise-robustness sweeps, head-count ablations, solver-order studies (bosh3/dopri5/dopri8), missingness robustness, a high-dimensional PEMS-SF scalability test, memory/VRAM comparisons against Mamba, and a smoothing-spline ablation that helps isolate the contribution of the attention mechanism from simple smoothing.
The reported speedups (4–14x) combined with accuracy improvements, if the baselines are correctly tuned, would represent a practically useful contribution for deploying Neural CDEs at scale.

The attention visualizations (Figure 5) provide a reasonable qualitative interpretability story distinguishing MV vs. MVC behavior across datasets with different characteristics (low-dim, high-dim, long sequences).
weaknesses: The reported Linear/Cubic Neural CDE baseline accuracies are substantially below what is reported in the original Neural CDE literature for the same UEA datasets (e.g., CharacterTrajectories typically reaches ~99% with cubic splines in prior work, but only 91.89% is reported here; SpokenArabicDigits baselines are similarly depressed). This large gap raises serious concerns that the spline baselines were under-tuned, which would artificially inflate the apparent gains of the proposed smoothing/attention method — a significant soundness issue that is not addressed or even acknowledged.

The experimental protocol explicitly gives Linear/Cubic CDE baselines the *same* fixed hyperparameters as the proposed method (Section B.4/B.6), while other baselines (ODE-RNN, GRU-D, Log-NCDE, Mamba) received dedicated hyperparameter searches. Since Linear/Cubic CDE is the most important comparison for isolating the effect of the proposed smoothing scheme, denying it independent tuning undermines the fairness and validity of the central claimed improvement.

Several "Theorem" statements (3.1, 3.2, 3.4) are largely direct restatements of well-known adaptive-solver local-truncation-error scaling arguments (Hairer et al., 1993) dressed up with formal theorem/proof structure; the derivations rely on loose big-O/≲ relations and informal chain-rule arguments (e.g., assuming ||dz/dt|| ∝ ||dX/dt|| without rigorously justifying the proportionality constant's boundedness across training), giving an impression of more mathematical rigor than is actually delivered.

The GP "optimality" proof (Appendix A.5) only shows GP is the optimal *linear* smoother under a *correctly specified* kernel and noise model; in practice the RBF kernel/hyperparameters are heuristically chosen and task-tuned, so the practical relevance of this optimality guarantee for the actual reported gains is unclear and somewhat oversold in the main text.

Many reported improvements have large overlapping error bars (e.g., UWaveGestureLibraryLinear NCDE: 86.82±4.22 vs. GP: 91.14±1.87), and no statistical significance testing is provided, making some claimed superiority difficult to substantiate rigorously.

The core methodological novelty (Q-Former-style learnable-query cross-attention over multiple smoothed/GP paths) is an incremental combination of existing ideas (kernel/GP path smoothing, multi-head attention, block-diagonal CDE integration from Structured Linear CDEs) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the paper's own related-work section acknowledges substantial overlap with several very recent architectures (Log-NCDE, Structured Linear CDEs, Attentive NCDEs).

Evaluation is restricted to three relatively small/simple UEA classification benchmarks as the "main" results, with a single small-scale forecasting experiment (ETTm1, 24-step horizon) relegated to a secondary role; broader comparisons to modern long-sequence/irregular time-series baselines beyond Mamba are absent, limiting confidence in the generality of the significance claims.
No code or artifact release is mentioned despite the highly detailed experimental setup, which limits independent verification of the concerning baseline-accuracy discrepancy noted above.
The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any limitations or risks specific to this work.

strengths: Clearly motivated problem: the paper correctly identifies that standard exact interpolation schemes (linear/cubic splines) drive NFE explosion in Neural CDEs by forcing the solver through noisy raw observations, and this is a real, practically important bottleneck for adopting Neural CDEs.

The proposed combination of kernel/GP smoothing with a Q-Former-style multi-view attention mechanism to recover information lost to smoothing is a sensible and reasonably novel architectural idea for this specific problem, even though the individual components (GP smoothing, cross-attention with learnable queries) are borrowed from existing literature.

Extensive empirical evaluation: three UEA classification benchmarks with multiple seeds, plus a large battery of appendix ablations (head count/diversity, bandwidth heterogeneity, solver order sensitivity, missingness rates, high-dimensional PEMS-SF scalability, memory footprint, forecasting under missingness, smoothing-spline baseline comparison). This breadth substantially strengthens the empirical case.

Consistent, sizeable improvements in both accuracy and NFE/training time are reported across datasets and are corroborated by multiple complementary analyses (noise robustness, missingness robustness, Pareto plots), rather than resting on a single headline number.

Reasonable effort toward fair comparison: baseline Linear/Cubic CDEs are parameter-matched and use the same optimization schedule as the proposed models, and solver-tolerance sweeps are provided so that baseline efficiency cannot be trivially matched by relaxing precision.
Honest limitations section that acknowledges solver dependency, bandwidth sensitivity, the multi-head "stiffest head" bottleneck, and loss of high-frequency information under smoothing.
weaknesses: The theoretical results (Theorem 3.1–3.4) are stated with imprecise ≲ scaling relations and rely on informal steps; in particular the claim that higher-order derivatives of the latent state z scale essentially linearly/proportionally with the same-order derivatives of the control path X (used to go from the LTE bound to Theorem 3.1) glosses over the fact that Neural CDE dynamics are governed by a nonlinear product rule (Faà di Bruno-type expansion), so higher derivatives of z generally depend on products of multiple lower-order derivatives of X and f, not simply on d^(p+1)X/dt^(p+1). This weakens the rigor of the central theoretical motivation, even though the qualitative intuition is reasonable and well supported empirically.

Theorem 3.4's proof assumes the adaptive solver enforces the error tolerance independently in every state-vector component (via an infinity-norm argument), but standard implementations (e.g., torchdiffeq's dopri5) typically use an RMS/L2-type combined norm across the state, which would not strictly enforce the stated per-head worst-case bottleneck in the same way; this assumption is not justified or tested against the actual solver norm used in experiments.

No direct empirical comparison against Neural Rough CDEs (Morrill et al., 2021), which is repeatedly discussed in Related Work as a competing algebraic approach to the same NFE problem, despite Log-NCDE being included; this omission leaves a gap in the empirical positioning relative to the closest class of prior efficiency methods.

The forecasting evaluation (Section 4.2) is limited to a single dataset (ETTm1) and a single missingness rate, which is a fairly narrow basis for the generative-forecasting claims made in the abstract/conclusion.

In the high-dimensional PEMS-SF experiment, MVC-GP is roughly 40× slower in wall-clock training time than Mamba (1679s vs 41s) despite higher accuracy; the abstract's framing of "performing competitively alongside... Mamba" somewhat understates this large absolute efficiency gap in favor of discrete state-space models on high-dimensional data.

Several cited works carry 2026 publication/forum years (e.g., Chevyrev & Kormilitzin, 2026; Kuleshov et al., 2026), which, while plausibly legitimate pending publications, are difficult for reviewers to verify and warrant double-checking for reference accuracy.

The paper does not report statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests) between the proposed method and the strongest baselines despite reporting standard deviations, leaving some accuracy gaps (e.g., MV vs MVC differences of 1-3%) without formal significance backing.
